chunks: BEMF speed sensing for motors and solenoids. The question: How can you use BEMF to measure motor/solenoid speed?
A spinning motor is also a generator. The voltage it generates, called back-EMF, is proportional to its speed.
So if you can read that voltage by itself, you have a speed sensor with no extra part. The trouble is that while current flows, other voltage drops hide it.
The usual fix is to measure when the current has stopped. For a solenoid the matching effect is weaker and depends on the plunger's position.
Think of a bicycle dynamo that lights a lamp. Pedal faster and the lamp gets brighter, because the dynamo makes more voltage at higher speed. A motor shaft acts like that dynamo.
To read it cleanly, you disconnect the power for an instant and measure what the spinning shaft produces on its own.
Switch Q₁ drives the motor from the battery; D₁ freewheels the motor current when Q₁ turns off.
A divider from the motor terminal to the ADC lets the MCU read the terminal voltage. During Q₁-off, once the diode current has stopped, that voltage equals the back-EMF.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, E equals K e omega . It is proportional to speed.
K e : the back-EMF constant, in volts per rad/s of speed (radians per second; one turn is 2π radians).
Off-time sampling: reading the terminal voltage while a PWM drive (one that switches on and off rapidly) is off and the current has died away.
Freewheel (flyback) diode: carries the winding's current after the switch opens.
A motor has K e equals 0. 02 volts per rad/s. At 3000 rpm, which is 314 rad/s, it generates 0. 02 times 314 equals 6. 28 volts. Turn the PWM switch off.
After the freewheel current dies, about 0. 13 milliseconds for a small example motor, the open terminal voltage is that 6. 28 volts.
Two resistors scale it down for the microcontroller's ADC (its voltage-to-number converter), and you divide by K e to get speed. At 300 rpm it is only 0.
63 volts, which is why the method struggles at low speed. That is the whole idea.
"Back-EMF is proportional to speed, E equals Ke omega.

The terminal voltage is IR plus L di/dt plus E, so I measure it when the current is zero: switch the drive off during the PWM off-time, wait for the freewheel current to decay, and sample the terminal through a divider into an ADC.
Speed is that voltage over Ke. Otherwise subtract the I times R drop during on-time. It fails at low speed and drifts with temperature, because R rises about 0. 4% per degree."
